Elements¶

Element classes. Every class also has a lowercase alias (svgwriter.circle is svgwriter.Circle).

Base classes¶

class Element(*children: Element | str, id: str | None = None, attrs: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None, **extra: Any)[source]¶

Bases: Construction, AttributeAccess, TreeEditing, Queryable, Displayable, Composable

Base class for every SVG element.

Attributes are kept in attributes under their SVG names; keyword arguments use Python spelling (stroke_width, class_, xlink_href) and are translated by svg_name().

Parameters:

  • *children (Element or str) – Child elements and text nodes.

  • id (str, optional) – The element id. Defaults to None.

  • attrs (mapping, optional) – Extra attributes given by their SVG names. Defaults to None.

  • **extra – Any other attribute, Python spelling.

Raises:

UnknownKeywordError – If a keyword is not a known SVG attribute.

See also

svgwriter.model.elements.Container

Elements that hold children.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> el = svg.rect(0, 0, 10, 10, stroke_width=2)
>>> el.tag, el.attributes["stroke-width"]
('rect', 2)

arranges_children: ClassVar[bool] = False¶

True for layout groups, which place their children before any child is measured.

namespace: ClassVar[str | None] = None¶

property animate: Any¶

el.animate.fade_in(1).spin(2, begin=1).

Returns:

Motion – Chainable presets that add SMIL animation children.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> _ = svg.rect(0, 0, 10, 10).animate.fade_in()
Type:

Animation presets for this element

property home: Element¶

a detached copy to start each frame from.

A behavior that sets the state from home (element.t = element.home.t, then a relative move) computes every frame afresh, so the motion never drifts and frames can be drawn in any order.

Returns:

Element – The copy Scene.attach took.

Raises:

ValueError – If no behavior has been attached to this element.

See also

svgwriter.catalog.preset.behavior

Write a behavior.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> class Hop(svg.Scene):
...     width, height, duration = 40, 40, 1.0
...     def build(self, doc):
...         self.dot = doc.circle(20, 30, 4).animate.hover(height=10).element
>>> scene = Hop()
>>> scene.dot.cy = 31
>>> float(scene.dot.home.cy)
30.0
Type:

The element as it was when its first behavior was attached

computed(name: str, default: object = None) → object[source]¶

The value SVG would use for property name (SVG spelling or Python spelling).

Looks at the inline style, matching <style> rules, the presentation attribute, then ancestors for inherited properties.

Parameters:

  • name (str) – Property name, in SVG (font-size) or Python (font_size) spelling.

  • default (object, optional) – Returned when the property is not set anywhere. Defaults to None.

Returns:

object – The property’s value, written as SVG text when it is not a plain number, or default.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> g = svg.group(fill="red", font_size=30)
>>> t = g.add(svg.text("hi", style="font-size: 12px"))
>>> t.computed("fill"), t.computed("font_size"), t.computed("opacity", 1)
('red', '12px', 1)
clone(linked: Literal[False] = False) → E[source]¶
clone(linked: Literal[True]) → Use

A deep, detached copy; or with linked, a <use> that renders this element.

Parameters:

linked (bool) – False copies the whole subtree (pixels included), so edits never reach the original. True returns a <use> referencing this element (giving it an id), so edits to the original show through every linked clone.

Returns:

Element – A copy of the same class, or a Use.

Notes

A linked clone needs the original in the same document: placed anywhere, or unplaced, in which case it moves into <defs> when the <use> joins the document. copy.copy and copy.deepcopy both behave like clone().

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> star = svg.circle(0, 0, 5, id="dot")
>>> star.clone().id, star.clone(linked=True).tag
('dot', 'use')
append(child: C) → C¶

Append a child element or text node and return it.

An element that already has a parent is moved. Elements referenced by the child but not yet placed are collected into the root <defs>.

Parameters:

child (Element or str) – The child to append.

Returns:

Element or str – The appended child.

Raises:

TypeError – If the content model forbids the child, or it is not an element or str.

See also

insert

Add a child at a given position.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> g = svg.group()
>>> g.append(svg.circle(0, 0, 1)).tag
'circle'

>>> len(g)

property iri: IRI¶

#id pointing at this element, assigning an id if needed.

Use it where SVG expects a plain IRI (xlink:href of <use>, <mpath>, …); passing the element itself does the same. An element’s own xlink:href is el.href.

See also

url

The url(#id) form.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> svg.rect(0, 0, 1, 1, id="a").iri.svg_value()

iter(tag: str | None = None, *, max_depth: float = inf) → Iterator[Element]¶

Depth-first walk over this element and its descendants.

Parameters:

  • tag (str, optional) – Yield only elements with this tag. Defaults to None (all).

  • max_depth (float, optional) – Deepest level to descend to; 0 is this element only. Defaults to infinity.

Yields:

Element – Elements in document order, starting with this one.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> g = svg.group(svg.circle(0, 0, 1), svg.rect(0, 0, 1, 1))
>>> [e.tag for e in g.iter()]
['g', 'circle', 'rect']
property label: str | None¶

A readable name for the element, stored as inkscape:label, or None.

Inkscape shows it in its Layers and Objects panels, and doc["name"] finds an element by label when no id matches. Assigning None removes it.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> r = svg.rect(0, 0, 1, 1)
>>> r.label = "Logo"
>>> r.label, r.attributes["inkscape:label"]
('Logo', 'Logo')

classmethod many(**columns: Any) → list[E]¶

Build many elements at once from columns that broadcast like numpy.

Each keyword is an attribute in Python spelling; a scalar applies to every element and an array gives one value per element. Colors may be one color, a list of colors or an (n, 3|4) array of 0-1 floats.

Parameters:

**columns – Attribute name to scalar or sequence.

Returns:

list of Element – The new elements, ready for doc.group(*elements) or doc.add_all.

Raises:

ValueError – If the columns do not broadcast to one length.

Examples

>>> import numpy as np
>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> dots = svg.Circle.many(cx=np.arange(3) * 10, cy=5, r=2, fill=["red", "green", "blue"])
>>> [str(d) for d in dots][1]
'<circle cx="10" cy="5" r="2" fill="green"/>'

set(name: str, value: AttrValue) → None¶

Set one attribute; None removes it.

Attributes in other namespaces use Clark notation: "{uri}name". Colors with alpha are split into the color and its *-opacity attribute, and elements are replaced by references to them. A presentation property the inline style already declares (as Inkscape writes them) is changed there, where it takes effect.

Parameters:

  • name (str) – The attribute name, Python or SVG spelling.

  • value (object) – The new value; None removes the attribute.

Raises:

  • TypeError – If a length, angle or ~svgwriter.Quantity has the wrong dimension for the attribute (width given an area).

  • ValueError – If the attribute is unsupported, a color string is not a valid color or paint, or a color with alpha is given to an attribute without an opacity counterpart.

See also

update

Set several attributes at once.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> r = svg.rect(0, 0, 1, 1)
>>> _ = r.set("stroke_width", 3)
>>> r.attributes["stroke-width"]
3
>>> styled = svg.rect(0, 0, 1, 1, style="fill:#ff0000")
>>> styled.fill = "blue"
>>> styled.attributes["style"], styled.has("fill")
(Style({'fill': 'blue'}), False)
property text_content: str¶

All character data below this element, in document order (the DOM textContent).

Assigning replaces every child with the single string.

>>> t[6:].fill = "red"
>>> t.text_content

>>> title = svg.Title("Old")
>>> title.text_content = "New"
>>> str(title)
'<title>New</title>'

class Transformable(*args: Element | str, t: Transform | TransformOp | Matrix | str | None = None, transform: Transform | TransformOp | Matrix | str | None = None, anchor: tuple[float, float] | Point | str | None = None, **kwargs: Any)[source]¶

Bases: Placement, TransformMethods, Element

An element placed by a transform.

The element’s own geometry attributes (cx, x, d, …) are local coordinates and stay as written; every move goes through t. Rotation, scaling and skewing pivot on anchor.

Parameters:

  • t (Transform, Matrix or str, optional) – Initial transform (transform= is accepted as an alias). Defaults to None.

  • anchor ((float, float), optional) – Pivot in local coordinates. Defaults to the bounding-box centre.

See also

svgwriter.model.elements._behavior.Convertible

Conversions and clipping on top of this class.

Notes

t is one affine matrix. Every method multiplies into it (before it in the parent frame, after it with local=True) instead of appending to a list; output is the shortest equivalent transform.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> c = svg.circle(50, 50, 10).translate(10, 0).rotate(90)
>>> str(c.t)
'rotate(90 55 55)'
>>> c.position
Point(x=60.0, y=50.0)
transform_attribute: ClassVar[str] = 'transform'¶
property t: Matrix¶

The transform as an affine Matrix; assign to replace it.

Written to SVG as the shortest equivalent transform text.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> svg.rect(0, 0, 1, 1).translate(2, 3).t.apply(0, 0)
Point(x=2.0, y=3.0)
property transform: Matrix¶

Same as t, under the SVG attribute’s name.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> r = svg.rect(0, 0, 1, 1).translate(2, 3)
>>> r.transform == r.t
True
local_bbox() → BBox | None[source]¶

Bounding box in local coordinates (before t), if known.

BBox or None – The box, or None when the element has no known extent. Subclasses override this.

class Convertible(*args: Element | str, t: Transform | TransformOp | Matrix | str | None = None, transform: Transform | TransformOp | Matrix | str | None = None, anchor: tuple[float, float] | Point | str | None = None, **kwargs: Any)[source]¶

Bases: Transformable

Conversions (to_path, to_group, rasterize) and clip.

Every conversion returns a new element or array and leaves this one unchanged. A conversion that cannot be done raises TypeError naming the element and the alternatives.

See also

svgwriter.model.elements.Transformable

Transforms and anchors.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> box = svg.rect(0, 0, 10, 5, fill="red")
>>> type(box.to_path()).__name__
'Path'
>>> box.rasterize().shape
(5, 10, 4)

Raises:

>>> svg.circle(5, 5, 2).to_path().tag
'path'

A group returns a copy of itself.

**kwargs – Attributes set on the group.

Returns:

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> g = svg.circle(5, 5, 2).to_group(opacity=0.5)
>>> g.tag, len(g)

to_image(*, scale: float = 1.0, padding: float = 0.0, background: ColorLike | None = None) → Image[source]¶

Rasterize into an <image> placed over this element’s bounds.

Parameters:

  • scale (float, optional) – Pixels per user unit. Defaults to 1.0.

  • padding (float, optional) – Extra margin in user units. Defaults to 0.0.

  • background (color, optional) – Painted under the element. Defaults to None (transparent).

Returns:

Image – Embedded pixels positioned where the element was drawn.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> img = svg.circle(10, 10, 5, fill="red").to_image(scale=2)
>>> img.shape, (img.x, img.y, img.width)
((20, 20), (5.0, 5.0, 10.0))
clip(*shapes: Element, units: str | None = None) → E[source]¶

Clip to the union of shapes (or a ClipPath) and return self.

Shapes are in this element’s local coordinates, so the clip moves with the element. The <clipPath> goes into <defs> when the element is in a document.

Parameters:

  • *shapes (Element) – Shapes, text or <use>; a single ClipPath is used as is.

  • units ({"userSpaceOnUse", "objectBoundingBox"}, optional) – clipPathUnits for a new clip path. Defaults to None.

Returns:

Convertible – This element.

Raises:

TypeError – If no shape is given.

See also

unclip

Remove the clip.

Notes

to_path() (or flatten_clip()) bakes the clip into one path with a boolean intersection.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> art = svg.rect(0, 0, 100, 100, fill="teal").clip(svg.circle(50, 50, 40))
>>> art.clip_region.tag
'clipPath'
unclip() → E[source]¶

Remove the clip and return self.

Returns:

Convertible – This element.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> art = svg.rect(0, 0, 9, 9).clip(svg.circle(4, 4, 3)).unclip()
>>> art.clip_region is None
True
property clip_region: ClipPath | None¶

The <clipPath> this element is clipped by, if it can be found.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> svg.rect(0, 0, 9, 9).clip_region is None
True
render_bounds() → BBox | None[source]¶

bounds() grown by half the stroke width.

Returns:

BBox or None – The box including the stroke, or None when bounds() is unknown.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> svg.rect(0, 0, 10, 10, stroke="black", stroke_width=2).render_bounds()
BBox(x=-1.0, y=-1.0, width=12.0, height=12.0)
rasterize(*, scale: float = 1.0, pixels: tuple[int, int] | int | None = None, padding: float = 0.0, background: ColorLike | None = None) → np.ndarray[source]¶

Render this element alone into an RGBA array.

The canvas is the element’s render_bounds() in parent coordinates, plus padding on every side.

Parameters:

  • scale (float, optional) – Pixels per user unit. Defaults to 1.0.

  • pixels ((int, int) or int, optional) – Exact output (columns, rows), or one int for a square; the element is fitted and centred, and scale is ignored. Defaults to None.

  • padding (float, optional) – Extra margin in user units. Defaults to 0.0.

  • background (color, optional) – Painted under the element. Defaults to None (transparent).

Returns:

numpy.ndarray – float32 array, shape (rows, columns, 4), straight RGBA in 0..1.

Raises:

TypeError – When the element’s size is unknown (an <image> without width and height, for instance).

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> svg.rect(0, 0, 8, 4, fill="red").rasterize(scale=2).shape
(8, 16, 4)
class PathOperand(*children: Element | str, id: str | None = None, attrs: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None, **extra: Any)[source]¶

Bases: BooleanOps, Measurement, AlongPath, Element

An element with an outline.

Adds to_path(), exact measurement, walking the outline (at(), sample(), between(), round_corners(), …) and boolean operators:

  • a | b: union

  • a & b: intersection

  • a - b: difference

  • a ^ b: exclusive or

Every operator returns a new Path carrying the left operand’s presentation attributes.

See also

svgwriter.model.elements._behavior.Convertible

Conversions and clipping.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> a, b = svg.rect(0, 0, 10, 10), svg.rect(5, 0, 10, 10)
>>> (a | b).exact_bbox().width, (a & b).exact_bbox().width
(15.0, 5.0)

Outline in the element’s own coordinates (t and clipping ignored).

PathData – The outline; subclasses override this.

TypeError – If the element has no outline.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> str(svg.rect(0, 0, 4, 3).local_outline())
'M0 0 H4 V3 H0 Z'
outline() → PathData[source]¶

Outline in parent coordinates: clipped by clip-path, then t applied.

Returns:

PathData – The outline.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> str(svg.rect(0, 0, 4, 3).translate(1, 1).outline())
'M1 1 L5 1 L5 4 L1 4 Z'
to_path(**kwargs: Any) → Path[source]¶

An equivalent <path> with t and any clip baked in.

Presentation attributes are copied; keywords override them.

Parameters:

**kwargs – Attributes set on the new path, overriding copied ones.

Returns:

Path – A new <path> element.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> svg.rect(0, 0, 4, 3, fill="red").to_path().get("fill")
'red'
flatten_clip() → Path[source]¶

The visible area as one <path>: to_path() with the clip applied.

Returns:

Path – A new <path> without clipping.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> art = svg.rect(0, 0, 10, 10).clip(svg.rect(0, 0, 5, 5))
>>> art.flatten_clip().exact_bbox().width
5.0
expand_pattern() → Element[source]¶

Replace a pattern fill by copies of its tile, clipped to this outline (plain vector graphics).

Useful for targets without pattern support (plotters, cutters, some editors). The stroke, if any, is kept on top.

Returns:

Group – A <g> with this element’s transform holding the clipped tiles and an unfilled copy for the stroke.

Raises:

ValueError – If fill is not a <pattern>.

See also

svgwriter.Pattern.tiles

The tiles on their own.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> dots = svg.Pattern(svg.circle(2, 2, 1), width=4, height=4, pattern_units="userSpaceOnUse")
>>> expanded = svg.rect(0, 0, 8, 8, fill=dots, stroke="black").expand_pattern()
>>> [e.tag for e in expanded], len(expanded[0][0])
(['g', 'rect'], 4)
transformed(transform: TransformLike) → Path[source]¶

A <path> with t and then transform baked into its coordinates.

Parameters:

transform (Transform, Matrix or str) – The transform applied after t.

Returns:

Path – A new <path> with no transform attribute.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> str(svg.rect(0, 0, 1, 1).transformed("translate(2 0)").d)
'M2 0 L3 0 L3 1 L2 1 Z'

Bases: PathCommands, Shape

<path>: an arbitrary outline described by path data.

Drawing methods append commands to d and return the path, so paths can be built fluently, and paths combine with the operators of PathOperand.

Parameters:

  • d (str, PathData, PathBuilder or iterable of commands, optional) – The path data. Defaults to an empty path.

  • path_length (float, optional) – Author’s computed total length. Defaults to None.

  • **kwargs – Presentation, core and other SVG attributes in Python spelling.

See also

Polyline

Straight segments from a point array.

svgwriter.PathBuilder

Build path data without an element.

Notes

p1 + p2 appends p2’s subpaths to a copy of p1; p += p2 does it in place, as do |=, &=, -= and ^= for the boolean operations.

Drawing methods append to d and return the path, so a path can be built fluently: path().move_to(0, 0).line_to(10, 0).close().

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> str(svg.Path().move_to(0, 0).line_to(10, 0).arc_to(5, 5, 10, 10).close().d)
'M0 0 L10 0 A5 5 0 0 1 10 10 Z'
>>> a = svg.Path("M0 0 H10", stroke="red")
>>> str(a + svg.Path("M0 5 H10"))
'<path d="M0 0 H10 M0 5 H10" stroke="red"/>'

  • name (str, optional) – SVG attribute name; derived from the Python name when omitted.

  • convert (callable, optional) – Applied to raw strings (for instance values read by the parser).

  • default (object, optional) – Returned when the attribute is not set. Defaults to None.

See also

LengthAttr

Attribute that reads lengths.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> svg.Rect.width.key
'width'
>>> svg.Rect(width=3, height=1).width
3.0
property connects: Connection | None¶

The objects this path joins as an Inkscape connector, or None for a plain path.

Assign (start, end) to attach the path to two elements (inkscape:connection-start and -end; it is redrawn as a straight line between their centres), or None to detach it.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> doc = svg.Document(100, 40)
>>> a, b = doc.circle(10, 20, 5), doc.circle(90, 20, 5)
>>> wire = doc.path(stroke="black")
>>> wire.connects = (a, b)
>>> wire.connects.start is a, str(wire.d)
(True, 'M10 20 L90 20')
property d: PathData¶

The path data; assign a string, PathData or builder.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> p = svg.Path("M0 0 L10 0")
>>> p.d = "M5 5 H20"
>>> str(p)
'<path d="M5 5 H20"/>'
property nodes: ndarray¶

All end and control points as an (N, 2) array; assign to move them.

Assigning rewrites d in absolute form. Broadcasting works as in numpy: p.nodes = p.nodes * [1, -1] + 5.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> p = svg.Path("M0 0 L10 0 L10 10")
>>> p.nodes = p.nodes + [1, 2]
>>> str(p.d)
'M1 2 L11 2 L11 12'
classmethod from_points(points: Iterable[tuple[float, float]], *, closed: bool = False, **kwargs: Any) → Self[source]¶

Create a path through a sequence of points.

Parameters:

  • points (iterable of tuple of float) – Vertices (x, y); the first starts the path.

  • closed (bool, optional) – Close the path back to the first point. Defaults to False.

  • **kwargs

  • Presentation

  • spelling. (core and other SVG attributes in Python)

Returns:

Path – The new path.

See also

Polyline

The same outline as a <polyline>.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> str(svg.Path.from_points([(0, 0), (5, 0), (5, 5)], closed=True))
'<path d="M0 0 L5 0 L5 5 Z"/>'
property bbox: BBox¶

Geometric bounding box of the path data; empty paths give a zero box.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> svg.Path("M0 0 L10 5").bbox
BBox(x=0.0, y=0.0, width=10.0, height=5.0)

classmethod regular(cx: float, cy: float, radius: float, sides: int = 6, **kwargs: Any) → Self[source]¶

Create the vertices of a regular polygon.

The first vertex is at the top and the rest follow clockwise.

  • cy (float) – Center.

  • radius (float) – Distance from the center to each vertex.

  • sides (int, optional) – Number of vertices. Defaults to 6.

Returns:

Polyline – The new element; on Polygon it is closed.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> str(svg.Polygon.regular(0, 0, 10, 4))
'<polygon points="0,-10 10,0 0,10 -10,0"/>'

Bases: RectConstructors, Shape

<rect>: an axis-aligned rectangle with optional rounded corners.

Giving only one of rx and ry uses it for both, and radii are clamped to half the width and height, as SVG specifies.

Parameters:

  • x (length, optional) – Top-left corner. Defaults to 0.

  • y (length, optional) – Top-left corner. Defaults to 0.

  • width (length) – Size; required, by position or as width= and height=.

  • height (length) – Size; required, by position or as width= and height=.

  • rx (length, optional) – Corner radii. Defaults to None.

  • ry (length, optional) – Corner radii. Defaults to None.

  • **kwargs – Presentation, core and other SVG attributes in Python spelling.

Raises:

TypeError – If width or height is not given (rect needs width).

See also

Circle

A circle from its center and radius.

Path

Arbitrary outlines.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> str(svg.Rect(1, 2, 3, 4, rx=1))
'<rect x="1" y="2" width="3" height="4" rx="1"/>'

Base class for the basic shapes and paths.

Every shape converts to a <path> (to_path()) and supports the geometric operators of PathOperand.

<a>: a hyperlink around graphics.

Parameters:

  • *children (Element) – Initial content.

  • href (str or Element, optional) – The link target. Defaults to None.

  • target (str, optional) – Where to open the link, such as "_blank". Defaults to None.

  • **kwargs – Presentation, core and other SVG attributes in Python spelling.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> str(svg.A(svg.Rect(0, 0, 5, 5), href="https://example.com"))
'<a xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://example.com"><rect x="0" y="0" width="5" height="5"/></a>'
local_bbox() → BBox | None[source]¶

Box around the link’s children.

Returns:

BBox or None – The union of the children’s bounding boxes, or None when empty.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> svg.A(svg.rect(0, 0, 5, 5), href="#x").local_bbox()
BBox(x=0.0, y=0.0, width=5.0, height=5.0)
local_outline() → PathData[source]¶

Union of the link’s children’s outlines.

Returns:

PathData – The combined outline of every child.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> svg.A(svg.rect(0, 0, 5, 5), href="#x").local_outline().bbox

<color-profile>: an ICC profile referenced by icc-color.

Parameters:

  • name (str) – Name used to refer to the profile from icc-color.

  • href (str, optional) – Location of the profile. Defaults to None.

  • local (str, optional) – Name of a locally installed profile. Defaults to None.

  • rendering_intent (str, optional) – Rendering intent, such as "perceptual". Defaults to None.

  • **kwargs – Presentation, core and other SVG attributes in Python spelling.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> str(svg.ColorProfile("sRGB", "srgb.icc"))
'<color-profile xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="srgb.icc" name="sRGB"/>'

Bases: GraphicsElement, XLinkAttributes, Positioned

<image>: embedded pixels (numpy) or a linked file.

Parameters:

  • source (array, str or None, optional) – A pixel array ((H, W), (H, W, 3) or (H, W, 4); floats in 0..1 or uint8) to embed, or a URL/path to link. Defaults to None.

  • x (length, optional) – Top-left corner. Defaults to None.

  • y (length, optional) – Top-left corner. Defaults to None.

  • width (length, optional) – Display size; defaults to the pixel size for embedded images.

  • height (length, optional) – Display size; defaults to the pixel size for embedded images.

  • alpha (array or float, optional) – Separate alpha, broadcastable to (H, W). Defaults to None.

  • preserve_aspect_ratio (PreserveAspectRatio or str, optional) – How the pixels fit the box. Defaults to None.

  • **kwargs – Presentation, core and other SVG attributes in Python spelling.

See also

Image.open

Embed an image file.

Pixels

The pixel container behind an embedded image.

Notes

color is float32 (H, W, C) (C is 1 for grayscale, else 3) and alpha is the scalar 1.0 when fully opaque, otherwise (H, W, 1), so color * alpha always broadcasts. Edit them in place or assign new arrays. Pixels are written as a PNG data: URI.

Examples

>>> import numpy as np
>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> img = svg.Image(np.zeros((2, 3, 3)), x=10)
>>> img.shape, img.width, img.alpha
((2, 3), 3.0, 1.0)
>>> img.color[..., 0] = 1.0
>>> img.rgba()[0, 0].tolist()
[1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0]
classmethod open(path: str | PathLike[str], **kwargs: Any) → Image[source]¶

Decode an image file into an embedded <image>.

Parameters:

  • path (str or os.PathLike) – A PNG, JPEG, WebP, GIF or BMP file.

  • **kwargs – Attributes for the image, as in the constructor.

Returns:

Image – An image holding the decoded pixels, sized to match them unless width and height are given.

Raises:

ValueError – If the file cannot be decoded.

Examples

>>> import os, tempfile
>>> import numpy as np
>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
...     name = os.path.join(folder, "pixel.png")
...     _ = open(name, "wb").write(svg.Image(np.zeros((2, 3, 3))).encode())
...     svg.Image.open(name).shape
(2, 3)
property pixels: Pixels | None¶

The embedded Pixels, or None for a linked image.

A data: URI read from a document is decoded on first use.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> svg.Image("photo.png").pixels is None
True
property color: ndarray¶

Color channels, float32 (H, W, 1|3) in 0..1; editable in place.

Assign an array to replace them.

Examples

>>> import numpy as np
>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> img = svg.Image(np.zeros((1, 2, 3)))
>>> img.color = np.ones((1, 2, 3))
>>> float(img.color.min())
1.0
property alpha: ndarray | float¶

1.0 when opaque, else float32 (H, W, 1).

Assign a scalar or an array broadcastable to (H, W) to replace it.

Examples

>>> import numpy as np
>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> img = svg.Image(np.zeros((2, 2, 3)))
>>> img.alpha = 0.5
>>> img.alpha.shape
(2, 2, 1)

class Pixels(color: ndarray | None, alpha: ndarray | float = 1.0, source: str | None = None)[source]¶

Bases: PixelCompositing, Drawable

Image data: color channels plus a broadcastable alpha.

color is (H, W, C) with C in {1, 3} and alpha broadcasts to it. Both are float32 in 0..1. A fully opaque image keeps alpha as the scalar 1.0. Written as a PNG data: URI.

Parameters:

  • color (numpy.ndarray or None) – float32 (H, W, 1|3) color channels; None when the pixels are still an undecoded data: URI.

  • alpha (numpy.ndarray or float, optional) – Opacity, 1.0 or an array broadcastable to color. Defaults to 1.0.

  • source (str, optional) – The data: URI to decode lazily when color is None. Defaults to None.

See also

Image

The <image> element holding pixels.

Examples

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from svgwriter.model.elements.structure import Pixels
>>> Pixels.from_array(np.zeros((2, 3, 3)))
Pixels(2x3, channels=3, opaque=True)
classmethod from_array(array: object, alpha: object = None) → Pixels[source]¶

Create pixels from an array, splitting off any embedded alpha channel.

Parameters:

  • array (array-like) – (H, W) or (H, W, 1|2|3|4) values, floats in 0..1 or uint8. Two and four channels carry alpha last.

  • alpha (array-like or float, optional) – Separate alpha broadcastable to (H, W). Defaults to None.

Returns:

Pixels – The color and alpha as float32 arrays.

Raises:

  • ValueError – If the shape is unsupported, float values leave 0..1, or alpha is given both in array and as alpha.

  • TypeError – If the array is not numeric.

Examples

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from svgwriter.model.elements.structure import Pixels
>>> px = Pixels.from_array(np.zeros((1, 2, 4)))
>>> px.color.shape, px.alpha.shape
((1, 2, 3), (1, 2, 1))
classmethod decode(data: bytes, *, profile: bytes | str | None = None, intent: str | None = None) → Pixels[source]¶

Decode encoded image bytes into sRGB.

Embedded colour information (ICC profile, PNG gAMA/cHRM) is applied, so the pixels look as the file intends. ICC profiles go through LittleCMS.

Parameters:

  • data (bytes) – PNG, JPEG, WebP, GIF, BMP or PNM file contents.

  • profile (bytes or str, optional) – The color-profile of the image: ICC profile bytes that replace any embedded profile, "sRGB" to read the stored values as sRGB, or "auto" (the default, also None) to use the embedded profile.

  • intent (str, optional) – SVG rendering-intent for a profile conversion, such as "relative-colorimetric". Defaults to perceptual.

Returns:

Pixels – The decoded pixels.

Raises:

ValueError – If the data is damaged or in an unknown format, or profile is an unknown keyword.

Examples

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from svgwriter.model.elements.structure import Pixels
>>> png = Pixels.from_array(np.zeros((2, 2, 3))).encode()
>>> Pixels.decode(png)
Pixels(2x2, channels=3, opaque=True)

<svg>: a document root or nested viewport.

Parameters:

  • *children (Element) – Initial content.

  • version (str, optional) – Written as the version attribute; None omits it. Defaults to the SVG version the library targets ("1.1").

  • base_profile (str, optional) – The remaining <svg>-specific attributes. Defaults to None.

  • zoom_and_pan (str, optional) – The remaining <svg>-specific attributes. Defaults to None.

  • content_style_type (str, optional) – The remaining <svg>-specific attributes. Defaults to None.

  • **kwargs – Position (x, y, width, height), view_box, presentation, conditional and core attributes in Python spelling.

See also

Group

Group content without establishing a viewport.

Symbol

A reusable viewport instantiated by <use>.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> str(svg.Svg(svg.Circle(5, 5, 3), width=10, height=10))
'<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="10" height="10" version="1.1"><circle cx="5" cy="5" r="3"/></svg>'
classmethod with_size(width: float, height: float, **kwargs: Any) → Self[source]¶

Create a root with a size and a matching viewBox.

Parameters:

  • width (float) – Size in user units; the viewBox is 0 0 width height unless view_box is passed in kwargs.

  • height (float) – Size in user units; the viewBox is 0 0 width height unless view_box is passed in kwargs.

  • **kwargs

  • Presentation

  • spelling. (core and other SVG attributes in Python)

Returns:

Svg – The new root.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> str(svg.Svg.with_size(100, 50))
'<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="100" height="50" viewBox="0 0 100 50" version="1.1"/>'
defs() → Defs[source]¶

Return the first <defs> child, creating one if needed.

A new <defs> is inserted before all other children.

Returns:

Defs – The existing or newly created <defs>.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> doc = svg.Svg()
>>> doc.defs() is doc.defs()
True
>>> str(doc)
'<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" version="1.1"><defs/></svg>'

local_bbox() → BBox | None[source]¶

Box around the switch’s children.

Returns:

BBox or None – The union of the children’s bounding boxes, or None when empty.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> svg.Switch(svg.rect(0, 0, 5, 5)).local_bbox()
BBox(x=0.0, y=0.0, width=5.0, height=5.0)

Union of the switch’s children’s outlines.

'<use xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" x="10" xlink:href="#dot"/>'

class Character(text: Text, index: int, start: int | None = None, stop: int | None = None)[source]¶

Bases: _Characters

A live handle on character index of a <text> (text[i]).

Parameters:

  • text (Text) – The text the character belongs to.

  • index (int) – Zero-based index into Text.characters.

Notes

Moves and rotations edit the text’s dx/dy/rotate lists, so the result is still selectable SVG text. Scale and skew have no per-character form in SVG; use Text.glyphs() for outlines that can be transformed freely.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> t = svg.text("abc", x=0, y=10)
>>> t[1].translate(0, -4).rotate(20)
Character('b', 1)
>>> t.dy, t.rotate_
((0.0, -4.0, 4.0), (0.0, 20.0, 0.0))
property index: int¶

Zero-based index of the character in the text.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> svg.text("abc", x=0, y=10)[2].index
2
property char: str¶

The character itself.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> svg.text("abc", x=0, y=10)[1].char
'b'
property position: Point¶

Baseline origin of the glyph in the text’s local coordinates.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> svg.text("abc", x=5, y=10)[0].position.y
10.0
property angle: float¶

Per-character rotation in degrees.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> t = svg.text("abc", x=0, y=10)
>>> _ = t[1].rotate(20)
>>> t[1].angle
20.0
class CharacterRange(text: Text, start: int, stop: int)[source]¶

Bases: _Characters

A live handle on characters [start, stop) of a <text> (text[a:b]).

Setting a presentation attribute on the range wraps it in a styled <tspan>.

Parameters:

  • text (Text) – The text the characters belong to.

  • start (int) – Index of the first character.

  • stop (int) – Index one past the last character.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> t = svg.text("Hello world", x=0, y=20)
>>> t[6:11].fill = "red"
>>> str(t)
'<text x="0" y="20">Hello <tspan fill="red">world</tspan></text>'

Bases: TextAccess, PathOperand, GraphicsElement, _TextLength, _TextPositioning

<text>: a run of graphics text, laid out with the installed fonts.

The element holds character data and nested tspan, tref, textPath and altGlyph children. Characters can be addressed, moved and outlined individually.

Parameters:

  • *content (str or Element) – Text runs and tspan/tref/textPath/altGlyph children.

  • x (length or sequence of length, optional) – Absolute and relative positions; a list positions successive characters.

  • y (length or sequence of length, optional) – Absolute and relative positions; a list positions successive characters.

  • dx (length or sequence of length, optional) – Absolute and relative positions; a list positions successive characters.

  • dy (length or sequence of length, optional) – Absolute and relative positions; a list positions successive characters.

  • rotate (float or sequence of float, optional) – Per-character rotation in degrees.

  • text_length (length, optional) – Target advance width of the text.

  • length_adjust ({"spacing", "spacingAndGlyphs"}, optional) – How text_length is met.

  • decoration (TextDecoration, optional) – Written as text-decoration.

  • **kwargs – Presentation, core and other SVG attributes in Python spelling.

See also

TSpan

A styled or repositioned sub-run.

TextPath

Text laid out along a path.

Notes

Text takes part in boolean operations through its glyph outlines (Rect(0, 0, 100, 40) - Text("Hi", ...)). text[i] is a live Character for character i (len(text) counts characters); glyphs() returns one outline path per character. The method rotate() rotates the whole element; the per-character SVG rotate list is text.rotate_.

Examples

>>> str(Text("Hi", x=10, y=20, decoration=TextDecoration.UNDERLINE))
'<text x="10" y="20" text-decoration="underline">Hi</text>'

class TextDecoration(*values)[source]¶

Bases: Flag

The text-decoration keywords, combinable with |.

Pass a member (or a combination) as the decoration argument of Text, TSpan or AltGlyph.

See also

Text

The element that takes the decoration argument.

Examples

>>> d = TextDecoration.UNDERLINE | TextDecoration.LINE_THROUGH
>>> d.svg_value()
'underline line-through'
NONE = 0¶
UNDERLINE = 1¶
OVERLINE = 2¶
LINE_THROUGH = 4¶
BLINK = 8¶
svg_value(precision: int = 4) → str[source]¶

Format the flags as a text-decoration attribute value.

Parameters:

precision (int, optional) – Unused; accepted so every attribute value shares one signature. Defaults to the library’s default precision.

Returns:

str – The space-separated keywords, or "none" when no flag is set.

Examples

>>> TextDecoration.NONE.svg_value()
'none'
>>> TextDecoration.OVERLINE.svg_value()
'overline'

Shared base of linear and radial gradients.

Holds the color stops and the attributes common to both kinds.

Parameters:

  • *stops (Stop) – Color stops.

LinearGradient

Gradient along a line.

RadialGradient

Gradient around a center.

>>> import svgwriter as svg

>>> isinstance(grad, svg.Gradient), len(grad)
(True, 2)

<marker>: arrowheads and other symbols at path vertices.

Parameters:

  • *children (Element) – The marker graphics.

  • ref_x (float, optional) – The point aligned with the vertex. Defaults to 0.

  • ref_y (float, optional) – The point aligned with the vertex. Defaults to 0.

  • marker_width (length, optional) – Viewport size.

  • marker_height (length, optional) – Viewport size.

  • marker_units ({"strokeWidth", "userSpaceOnUse"}, optional) – Coordinate system of the size.

  • orient (float or "auto", optional) – Rotation; "auto" follows the path direction.

  • **kwargs – Presentation, core and other SVG attributes in Python spelling.

See also

Path

A shape that can carry markers.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> m = Marker(svg.Circle(0, 0, 2), ref_x=1, marker_width=4, marker_height=4, orient="auto")
>>> m.get("orient")
'auto'

<radialGradient>: a gradient around a center.

Parameters:

  • *stops (Stop) – Color stops.

  • cx (length, optional) – Center of the outer circle.

  • cy (length, optional) – Center of the outer circle.

  • r (length, optional) – Radius of the outer circle.

  • fx (length, optional) – Focal point.

  • fy (length, optional) – Focal point.

  • gradient_units ({"objectBoundingBox", "userSpaceOnUse"}, optional) – Coordinate system of the circle.

  • spread_method ({"pad", "reflect", "repeat"}, optional) – What happens beyond the circle.

  • **kwargs – Presentation, core and other SVG attributes in Python spelling.

See also

LinearGradient

Gradient along a line.

Examples

>>> str(RadialGradient(cx=0.5, cy=0.5, r=0.5))
'<radialGradient cx="0.5" cy="0.5" r="0.5"/>'

Box of the gradient’s outer circle.

Returns:

BBox or None – The unit box for objectBoundingBox units, otherwise the circle’s box.

Examples

>>> RadialGradient(cx=5, cy=5, r=2, gradient_units="userSpaceOnUse").local_bbox().width
4.0

  • blue (FeFunc, optional) – Functions for one channel each; they are converted to the matching feFuncR/G/B/A element. Default to None.

'<feComponentTransfer><feFuncR type="linear" slope="2" intercept="0"/></feComponentTransfer>'

Bases: SingleInput

<feConvolveMatrix>: apply a convolution kernel.

Parameters:

  • kernel_matrix (sequence of float, optional) – The kernel, row by row. Defaults to empty.

  • order (int or tuple of int, optional) – Kernel size, or (columns, rows). Defaults to 3.

  • divisor (float, optional) – Normalisation divisor and added bias. Default to None.

  • bias (float, optional) – Normalisation divisor and added bias. Default to None.

  • target_x (int, optional) – Kernel cell aligned with the output pixel. Default to None.

  • target_y (int, optional) – Kernel cell aligned with the output pixel. Default to None.

  • edge_mode (EdgeMode, optional) – Handling of pixels beyond the edge. Defaults to None.

  • kernel_unit_length (float or tuple of float, optional) – Kernel scale. Defaults to None.

  • preserve_alpha (bool, optional) – Leave the alpha channel unconvolved. Defaults to None.

  • **kwargs – Sub-region (x, y, width, height), result, in_ and other SVG attributes in Python spelling.

Raises:

ValueError – If the kernel length does not match order.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> str(svg.FeConvolveMatrix([0, 1, 0, 1, -4, 1, 0, 1, 0], divisor=1))
'<feConvolveMatrix order="3" kernelMatrix="0 1 0 1 -4 1 0 1 0" divisor="1"/>'

the direction is the same everywhere.

Type:

Always True

light_vector(x: float, y: float, z: float) → tuple[float, float, float][source]¶

The constant unit vector towards the light, independent of the point.

Parameters:

  • x (float) – The surface point; ignored, since the light is infinitely far away.

  • y (float) – The surface point; ignored, since the light is infinitely far away.

  • z (float) – The surface point; ignored, since the light is infinitely far away.

Returns:

tuple of float – Unit vector (x, y, z) pointing at the light.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> svg.FeDistantLight(0, 0).light_vector(5, 5, 0)
(1.0, 0.0, 0.0)

Bases: CoreAttributes

Shared base of the four channel transfer functions.

Parameters:

  • type (TransferType, optional) – Kind of function. Defaults to TransferType.IDENTITY.

  • table_values (sequence of float, optional) – Lookup table for table and discrete. Defaults to None.

  • slope (float, optional) – Coefficients of linear. Default to None.

  • intercept (float, optional) – Coefficients of linear. Default to None.

  • amplitude (float, optional) – Coefficients of gamma. Default to None.

  • exponent (float, optional) – Coefficients of gamma. Default to None.

  • offset (float, optional) – Coefficients of gamma. Default to None.

  • **kwargs – Core and other SVG attributes in Python spelling.

See also

FeComponentTransfer

The primitive that holds these functions.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> str(svg.FeFuncR.linear(2, 0.1))
'<feFuncR type="linear" slope="2" intercept="0.1"/>'
classmethod linear(slope: float, intercept: float = 0, **kwargs: Any) → Self[source]¶

Create a linear transfer function, slope * C + intercept.

Parameters:

  • slope (float) – Multiplier.

  • intercept (float, optional) – Added constant. Defaults to 0.

  • **kwargs – Core and other SVG attributes in Python spelling.

Returns:

FeFunc – The new function element.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> str(svg.FeFuncA.linear(0.5))
'<feFuncA type="linear" slope="0.5" intercept="0"/>'
classmethod table(*values: float, **kwargs: Any) → Self[source]¶

Create a piecewise-linear transfer function from lookup values.

Parameters:

  • *values (float) – Table entries, evenly spaced over the input range.

  • **kwargs – Core and other SVG attributes in Python spelling.

Returns:

FeFunc – The new function element.

See also

evaluate

Apply the function to a value.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> str(svg.FeFuncR.table(0, 1))
'<feFuncR type="table" tableValues="0 1"/>'
classmethod gamma(amplitude: float = 1, exponent: float = 1, offset: float = 0, **kwargs: Any) → Self[source]¶

Create a gamma transfer function, amplitude * C ** exponent + offset.

Parameters:

  • amplitude (float, optional) – Multiplier. Defaults to 1.

  • exponent (float, optional) – Power applied to the channel. Defaults to 1.

  • offset (float, optional) – Added constant. Defaults to 0.

  • **kwargs – Core and other SVG attributes in Python spelling.

Returns:

FeFunc – The new function element.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> svg.FeFuncG.gamma(2, 3).evaluate(0.5)
0.25
evaluate(c: float) → float[source]¶

Apply this transfer function to a channel value.

Parameters:

c (float) – Channel value in 0..1.

Returns:

float – The transformed value.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> svg.FeFuncR.linear(2, 0.1).evaluate(0.5)
1.1

<filter>: a graph of filter primitives.

Parameters:

  • *primitives (FilterPrimitive) – The primitives, in evaluation order.

  • filter_units ({"userSpaceOnUse", "objectBoundingBox"}, optional) – Coordinate systems for the region and the primitives.

  • primitive_units ({"userSpaceOnUse", "objectBoundingBox"}, optional) – Coordinate systems for the region and the primitives.

  • filter_res (float or (float, float), optional) – Intermediate image resolution.

  • **kwargs – Region (x, y, width, height), href and presentation/core attributes in Python spelling.

See also

FilterPrimitive

Base of the elements a filter contains.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> str(svg.Filter(svg.FeGaussianBlur(std_deviation=1), id="soft"))
'<filter id="soft"><feGaussianBlur stdDeviation="1"/></filter>'
collect() → Self[source]¶

Insert every detached primitive the filter’s primitives read, before its first reader.

Filter(merge) is then enough: the blur and offset that feed the merge come along in dependency order.

Returns:

Filter – This filter, for chaining.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> blur = svg.FeGaussianBlur(3, in_="SourceAlpha")
>>> shadow = svg.FeOffset(2, 2, in_=blur)
>>> f = svg.Filter(svg.FeMerge(shadow, "SourceGraphic"))
>>> [p.tag for p in f.primitives]
['feGaussianBlur', 'feOffset', 'feMerge']
property primitives: list[FilterPrimitive]¶

The filter-primitive children in evaluation order.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> svg.Filter(svg.FeOffset(), svg.FeTile()).primitives
[<FeOffset feOffset dx='0' dy='0'>, <FeTile feTile>]

sources() → list[FilterPrimitive][source]¶

The primitives this one reads, directly or through merge nodes, nearest first.

list of FilterPrimitive – Every upstream primitive given as an input object (not by name).

>>> import svgwriter as svg

>>> shifted = svg.FeOffset(2, 2, in_=blur)
>>> shifted.sources() == [blur]
True

resolve_input(value: StandardInput | str | FilterPrimitive | None) → StandardInput | str | None[source]¶

Turn a primitive into the name of its result.

Referring to a primitive by element lets its result name be generated on demand; keywords and strings pass through unchanged.

Parameters:

value (StandardInput, str, FilterPrimitive or None) – An input keyword, a result name or the primitive producing the input.

Returns:

StandardInput, str or None – The result name for a primitive, otherwise value itself.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> svg.resolve_input(svg.FeOffset(id="shift"))
'shift-out'
>>> svg.resolve_input("SourceAlpha")
'SourceAlpha'

class Animate(*args: Child, begin: Clock | None = None, dur: Clock | None = None, end: Clock | None = None, min: Clock | None = None, max: Clock | None = None, restart: Restart | None = None, repeat_count: RepeatCount | None = None, repeat_dur: Clock | None = None, fill: AnimationFill | None = None, values: Sequence[Any] | str | None = None, from_: Any = None, to: Any = None, by: Any = None, calc_mode: CalcMode | None = None, key_times: Sequence[float] | str | None = None, key_splines: Sequence[tuple[float, float, float, float]] | str | None = None, additive: Additive | None = None, accumulate: Accumulate | None = None, ease: EaseLike | None = None, attribute_name: str | None = None, attribute_type: Literal['CSS', 'XML', 'auto'] | None = None, href: str | Element | None = None, xlink_title: str | None = None, xlink_show: str | None = None, xlink_actuate: str | None = None, xlink_role: str | None = None, xlink_arcrole: str | None = None, required_features: str | Sequence[str] | None = None, required_extensions: str | Sequence[str] | None = None, system_language: str | Sequence[str] | None = None, external_resources_required: bool | None = None, xml_base: str | None = None, xml_lang: str | None = None, xml_space: XmlSpace | None = None, id: str | None = None, attrs: Mapping[str, AttrValue] | None = None, **kwargs: Any)[source]¶

Bases: FadeShortcut, AnimationElement, _ValueAnimation, _AttributeTarget

<animate>: interpolate one attribute over time.

Parameters:

  • attribute_name (str, optional) – The attribute to animate.

  • attribute_type ({"CSS", "XML", "auto"}, optional) – Namespace of the attribute.

  • values (sequence or str, optional) – The values to pass through.

  • from (object, optional) – Start value (written from).

  • to (object, optional) – End value.

  • by (object, optional) – Relative change.

  • calc_mode (CalcMode, optional) – Interpolation mode.

  • key_times (sequence of float or str, optional) – Times of each value, 0 to 1.

  • key_splines (sequence of 4-tuples or str, optional) – Bezier control points for spline mode.

  • additive (Additive, optional) – Combination with the underlying value.

  • accumulate (Accumulate, optional) – Whether repeats accumulate.

  • ease (str, tuple, callable or Ease, optional) – Timing curve over the whole timeline (see Ease); sets calcMode, keyTimes and keySplines (or samples values), so leave calc_mode unset or "linear"/"discrete".

  • **kwargs – Timing (begin, dur, repeat_count and so on, see AnimationElement), core and other SVG attributes.

See also

Set

Assign a value instead of interpolating.

AnimateTransform

Animate the transform attribute.

Examples

>>> str(Animate.fade(1, 0, dur=2))
'<animate attributeName="opacity" from="1" to="0" dur="2s"/>'
>>> str(Animate(attribute_name="x", from_=0, to=90, dur=1, ease="ease-in-out"))

class Ease(curve: Ease | str | tuple[float, float, float, float] | tuple[Any, ...] | Callable[[float], float] = 'linear')[source]¶

Bases: object

A timing curve: how an animation’s progress runs over its duration.

Every animation element and every element.animate preset takes one as ease=, in any of the forms below, and the curve applies to the whole timeline: with several values the motion through all of them follows the one curve (keyTimes are moved accordingly). Bézier curves are written as SMIL calcMode="spline" with exact keySplines; steps as calcMode="discrete"; a Python function is sampled into values with keyTimes at 24 to 60 evenly spaced times, more the more the curve bends, and played linearly between them.

Parameters:

curve (str, tuple, callable or Ease, optional) –

One of

  • a name: "linear" (the default), "ease", "ease-in", "ease-out", "ease-in-out" (the standard cubic-bézier curves), "step-start" or "step-end";

  • (x1, y1, x2, y2): a cubic bézier from (0, 0) to (1, 1) with 0 <= x1, x2 <= 1; y beyond 0..1 overshoots (and is then sampled, since SMIL splines stay inside the unit square);

  • ("steps", n) or ("steps", n, "start"): n equal jumps, at the end (default) or the start of each interval;

  • a function from time 0..1 to progress, normally 0..1 but free to overshoot (f(0) should be 0 and f(1) 1);

  • another Ease.

Raises:

  • ValueError – For an unknown name, a bézier x outside 0..1 or a step count below 1.

  • TypeError – For anything else.

See also

Animate

Takes ease.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> svg.Ease("ease-in")(0.5) < 0.5
True
>>> slide = svg.Animate(attribute_name="x", from_=0, to=100, dur=1, ease="ease-out")
>>> slide.get("keySplines"), slide.get("calcMode")
('0 0 0.58 1', 'spline')
>>> svg.Ease(("steps", 4))(0.6)
0.5
>>> svg.Ease(lambda t: t * t)(0.5)
0.25

Notes

Progress at time x along a bézier is found by solving x(s) = x for the curve parameter with Newton’s method, falling back to bisection, the same way the SMIL evaluator behind doc.at plays keySplines.

property linear: bool¶

Whether the curve is the identity, so it changes nothing.

time_of(progress: float) → float[source]¶

The earliest time (0..1) at which the curve reaches progress.

Parameters:

progress (float) – Target progress.

Returns:

float – The time, or 1.0 when the curve never gets there.

Examples

>>> round(Ease("ease-in").time_of(0.5), 3)
0.657
smil(values: Sequence[str], key_times: Sequence[float] | None = None, *, discrete: bool = False) → dict[str, Any][source]¶

SMIL timing attributes that play values along this curve over the whole timeline.

Parameters:

  • values (sequence of str) – The animation’s values.

  • key_times (sequence of float, optional) – Their times, evenly spread when omitted.

  • discrete (bool, optional) – Whether the animation jumps between values (calcMode="discrete"). Defaults to False.

Returns:

dict – Some of values, key_times, key_splines and calc_mode, in Python spelling; empty for a linear curve.

Examples

>>> Ease("ease-in").smil(["0", "10", "20"])["key_times"]
[0.0, 0.6575, 1.0]

Animation presets¶

element.animate returns a Motion; its methods add SMIL children and chain. @svg.preset.animation adds presets of your own as more methods, and Motion.apply runs any animation function with typed options (see Preset functions).

class Motion(element: Element)[source]¶

Bases: TransformPresets

Animation presets for one element; every method adds SMIL children and returns self to chain.

Reach it as element.animate. The SMIL plays in browsers, and svgwriter.Document.at(), video export and animated GIF/APNG/WebP play it too. Each preset takes dur (seconds), begin (seconds), repeat (a count, or "indefinite"), freeze (keep the end state; default True) and ease, a timing curve over the whole preset (a name such as "ease-in-out", a bézier 4-tuple, ("steps", n) or a function; see Ease). show and hide act at one instant, so they take only the moment. Presets added with @svg.preset.animation are methods too, and so are behaviors (@svg.preset.behavior), which attach to the scene owning the element.

Parameters:

element (Element) – What to animate.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> dot = svg.circle(10, 10, 5, fill="red")
>>> _ = dot.animate.fade_in(0.5).spin(2, begin=0.5)
>>> [child.tag for child in dot.children]
['animate', 'animateTransform']
>>> _ = dot.animate.move_to(80, 10, ease="ease-in-out")
>>> dot.children[-1].get("keySplines")
'0.42 0 0.58 1'
element¶
apply(function: ~collections.abc.Callable[[~typing.Concatenate[~svgwriter.model.elements._motion.Motion, ~P]], ~svgwriter.model.elements._motion.Motion | None], *args: ~typing.~P, **kwargs: ~typing.~P) → Motion[source]¶

Run an animation function on this element: function(self, *args, **kwargs).

Typed with the function’s own parameters, so editors complete and check its options. The function need not be registered; @svg.preset.animation also makes it element.animate.<name>.

Parameters:

  • function (callable) – function(motion, *, option=default, ...) returning the motion or None.

  • *args – Passed on to function.

  • **kwargs – Passed on to function.

Returns:

Motion – This motion, to chain further presets.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> def lift(motion: svg.Motion, *, height: float = 8) -> svg.Motion:
...     return motion.move_by(0, -height)
>>> dot = svg.circle(0, 0, 2)
>>> dot.animate.apply(lift, height=3).fade_in().element is dot
True

Draw the stroke on from its start, as if by a pen (dash offset from full length to 0).

create(dur: float = 1.0, *, begin: float = 0.0, freeze: bool = True, ease: Ease | str | tuple[float, float, float, float] | tuple[Any, ...] | Callable[[float], float] | None = None) → Motion[source]¶

Draw the outline on, then fade the fill in; a group creates every child at once.

A shape without a stroke is drawn with its fill color. Every contour starts drawing together, at the same pen speed. ease shapes the drawing and the fade each.

color_cycle(colors: list[Any], dur: float = 1.0, *, attribute: str = 'fill', begin: float = 0.0, repeat: float | str | None = 'indefinite', ease: Ease | str | tuple[float, float, float, float] | tuple[Any, ...] | Callable[[float], float] | None = None) → Motion[source]¶

morph(target: Element, dur: float = 1.0, *, begin: float = 0.0, repeat: float | str | None = None, freeze: bool = True, ease: EaseLike | None = None) → Motion[source]¶

Turn this <path>’s outline into target’s, matching their segments first.

Both outlines are brought to the same commands and segment count, so the d attribute can be interpolated; the path’s own d is rewritten to the matched start shape, which looks the same.

Parameters:

  • target (Element) – Any shape with an outline (<rect>, <circle>, <path>…).

  • dur (float, optional) – Seconds the morph takes. Defaults to 1.0.

  • begin (float, optional) – Seconds before it starts. Defaults to 0.0.

  • repeat (float or str, optional) – repeatCount: a number or "indefinite". Defaults to None (once).

  • freeze (bool, optional) – Keep the target shape after the end. Defaults to True.

  • ease (str or callable, optional) – Easing name or curve. Defaults to None (linear).

Returns:

Motion – This object, for chaining.

Raises:

TypeError – If the element is not a <path>; convert it with to_path() first.

See also

svgwriter.interpolate

The segment matching and blending used here.

Examples

>>> import svgwriter as svg
>>> shape = svg.rect(0, 0, 20, 20).to_path()
>>> _ = shape.animate.morph(svg.circle(10, 10, 10), 2)
>>> anim = shape.find(svg.Animate)
>>> anim.get("attributeName"), anim.get("dur")
('d', '2s')
>>> svg.circle(0, 0, 1).animate.morph(shape)
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
TypeError: morph animates a <path>'s d; convert first with element.to_path()
